2.text: caw like ravens, or bark like foxes, three times. This is done to conceal

3.text: their identity and to make it appear that they are ravens or foxes.

4.text: Then they begin to break the thong and to cut the clothes of the

5.text: corpse, replacing each piece with a slice of meat, until the whole body is

6.text: incased in this new covering. The face is covered with the duodenum. A

7.text: long piece of the thong is untied. This the “fortifier” winds around his waist,

8.text: and takes home to perform an incantation over it. Last of all, the pieces of

9.text: clothing are pulled from beneath the corpse. All the pieces cut off are laid

10.text: together at the right side of the body. The things brought along for the

11.text: personal use of the dead — such as the pipe, the knife, etc. — are also

12.text: left on the ground near the body. It is interesting to note that, among other

13.text: things, a small wooden image of a canoe is often left there. The Chukchee

14.text: say that it serves the deceased for that part of his journey which must be

15.text: made by water. The Reindeer Chukchee in actual life, however, have very

16.text: little occasion to use the canoe, at least in the interior of the country.

17.text: The sledge, the harness, and the traces are also cut and broken, and

18.text: the pieces are added to the heap. I was told that the sledges might be left

19.text: whole, but that they were broken lest the Russians or the Tungus should

20.text: take them away from the funeral place. Indeed, I know of cases where
20.note: mz draft reads "Indéed" with an accent over the e; at 2x the mark is a small ink speck above the e, not a diacritic — the printed word is the ordinary English "Indeed". class: draft.

21.text: whole sledges and other objects which were left near the corpse were really

22.text: appropriated by the people of “alien” tribes. One cossack on the Lower

23.text: Kolyma told me that, in one of his travels over the tundra, he took from

24.text: the funeral place of a Chukchee woman a cup and saucer of cheap china and

25.text: an iron scraper. The next night the woman appeared to him in a dream

26.text: and begged for her property. He was so affected by that dream, that he

27.text: returned to the funeral place, from which he had already travelled thirty

28.text: miles, and restored the stolen goods. The Russianized natives of the Kolyma

29.text: who accompanied me always showed an inclination to rob the Chukchee

30.text: funeral places of everything useful, but without any such scruples as those

31.text: described above, and it was difficult for me to prevent them from so doing.

32.text: On the other hand, in the camps on the Chukchee Peninsula and in the

33.text: Maritime villages, where there is no danger of theft from the funeral places,

34.text: the things left with the deceased are nevertheless very frequently broken or

35.text: spoiled, as, indeed, is done by many other tribes at funerals.

36.text: The carcasses of the reindeer are left on the spot, and the two sets of

37.text: antlers are placed at some distance from the body, one on either side of the

38.text: head. Then the “fortifier,” or the nearest relative of the deceased, proceeds

39.text: to rip up the body. He does it with a long knife, carefully avoiding to

40.text: touch the body with his hands, though they are protected with mittens or

41.text: with gloves of special form; that is, those with three fingers only. With two

42.text: strokes of the knife, which cross each other, the “fortifier” opens the breast, and
